items.title: ONE token turned a $0.40 AI request into $0.80.
items.summary:
ONE token turned a $0.40 AI request into $0.80.

and 4 "cheap" $20 subscriptions quietly cost $1,080 a year.

so i wrote 98 lines of python to audit what AI actually costs. real published prices, no vibes.

it said cut $360. the cache line alone was -88%.

here's what nobody checks.

ChatGPT Plus $20. Claude Pro $20. SuperGrok $30. Cursor Pro $20.
$90 a month. $1,080 a year. before tax.

each one looks reasonable the day you click subscribe. the bill only shows up when they stack

what the script printed, prices as of Aug 28, US web:

> 5M input + 1M output tokens a month: Sonnet 5 $20.00, Grok 4.6 $16.00, GPT-5.6 Luna $2.20
> use 1/5 of that and Sonnet is $4. not $20
> keep 2 subs + a $20 API budget: $720/yr. saves $360
> agent sending the same 100K prompt 50 times: $10.00 naive, $1.23 cached. -88%
> batch API: half price if you can wait
> Grok 4.6 at 199,999 tokens: $0.40. at 200,000: $0.80. one token doubles the whole request
> 20K records to JSON: $160 on Sol, $8.80 on Luna (my assumption: 1K in / 200 out each)

the lesson isn't "API is cheaper". heavy users burn $20 of API in days. the lesson is most people never did the math

how to audit yours:
1. list every AI sub and what you actually use it for
2. split the product (IDE, bots, connectors) from the model access
3. log 30 days of how often you open each one
4. move the occasional ones to pay-per-token
5. cache stable prompts, batch what can wait, watch the 200K / 272K cliffs
6. route easy work to cheap models, keep the frontier one for hard problems

every subscription has to earn its spot on your card. my math on published prices, not financial advice

i won't say anything more:

items.title: Fable5.2 ロールアウト!!
items.summary:
Fable5.2 ロールアウト!!
すでに全員使える状態です!!
注目すべきベンチスコア等について解説します～
Opus5.5でやった方が良いことも多々あるので公式推奨の使い分けも書きます

■スコアが上がった重要ベンチ
実案件をもとにした成果物づくり（RLI）17.9% → 41.3%  ※1

RLIベンチは実際のフリーランス案件をもとに、AIの成果物が人間の納品物と同等以上と判定された割合で、5.1の約2.3倍です。

つまり、仕事の仕様を渡して丸投げで質の高い成果物を出す割合が大幅に上がったということで、EQや視野の広さ、仕様を満たす要件の詰め方やクオリティを詰める能力が上がった可能性が高いです。

・ハードウェア設計 44.4 → 83.5%
Opus 5.5 は65.3。
公式が一段落のプロンプトから基板・筐体・ソフトまで作り、3つの電子機器を動作させた事例も出しています。AI×ハードウェア革命、く、くる…。

・実務コーディング 32.4% → 49.1%
OSSのメンテナにマージされるコードを書けるかを見るテストで、公開済みモデルでは最高。これはかなり気が効いてないと難しいので、気の利いたコードがかけるようになってる説

■ほかにも大きく伸びたベンチ（5.1 → 5.2）
・ロボット操作 27.6% → 64.9%
　GPT-6 Astra（29.8%）の2倍超
・業務フロー自動化 31.4% → 51.4%
・科学研究のエージェント作業 52.6% → 74.6%
・グラフ読み取り44.8% → 73.4%

■そこまで伸びていないベンチ
・PC操作：89.3%で、Opus 5.5とほぼ同じ
・知的業務：人間が見比べるEloでは1785で、Opus 5.5（1800）のほうがわずかに上。おーん
・AutomationBenchとChartography：5.1から大きく伸びたが、Gemini 4 Carbonとはほぼ横並びか負けです。
・AI研究開発（カーネル最適化・LLM設計）：安全上の理由で、訓練時にあえてOpus 5.5並みに抑えたと公式が明言。
・サイバー・生物：Fableでは大半のタスクが分類器でブロック、この分野をやるならMythos（審査制）が必要。

■価格と速度
- 入力トークンあたり$8/M：$10から低下
- 出力トークンあたり$40/M：$50から低下
- 20%安価
- 最大30%高速化

安くて速くなった？何が起きてる。

■Opus 5.5との使い分け
公式の推奨は「まずOpus 5.5から始め、足りなければFableへ上げる」。

□Opus 5.5がいい時
・日常のコーディングや調べもの、文章作業
・トークン単価が半分なので、量が多い作業
・セキュリティ系の作業

□Fable 5.2がいい時
・Opus 5.5をHigh/Maxにしても届かない難しい問題
・仕様が曖昧な丸投げ、何時間も走る長いエージェント作業
・多数のサブエージェントを指揮する作業
・Opusに作業させ、詰まった時だけFableに相談する「Advisor」構成も公式に案内

スコア見ても
普段使い　→　Opus5.5
丸投げ、大規模改修　→　Fable5.2
って感じはする。意外と主要スコアはOpus5.5からそれほど変わらないものも多いので。
エフォートはHighが一番コスパ良さそう

■Fable 5.5はまだ控えている？
・Azureのカタログに「claude-fable-5-5」の行が一時的に出た（10/13、数日で削除）
・Cursorが「fable-5.5」のモデルIDに対応した（10/17）
・パートナー企業にFable 5.5のチェックポイントが配られた、というリーク（TestingCatalog 10/17、11/1）
みたいなことがあったので、5.2が出て皆「！？」ってなってますね。

上場も控えていることですし、そのタイミングで最強の5.5を出す可能性はあり。

5.2はそのための繋ぎっぽさもあるけど、丸投げ系タスク、長時間タスク、大規模タスクには現時点最強と言って良いスコアなのでバンバン使っていって良さそう

Fableリセットっていう謎チケットも配布されてたので、5.5を待たずに早速私は自分のプロジェクトに使って行くことにするぜ

items.title: Accurate medical advice from AI can still be dangerous | STAT
items.summary: Artificial intelligence is delivering health guidance at an unprecedented scale. Every week, more than 300 million people ask ChatGPT health questions. Now, the federal government is moving AI deeper into medical care to communicate directly and autonomously with patients. Chris Klomp, the nominee for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, has called AI in patient care the agency’s “holy grail” for improving the nation’s health. [...] Medical ethics pairs the duty to do no harm with beneficence, which is an affirmative obligation to do good. Safety evaluations of AI have focused mainly on the first duty by screening for responses that encourage imminent self-harm, discourage necessary care, or spread false information. Behavioral benchmarking would extend the first duty beyond imminent danger to long-term harms. It could also advance the second duty, which has received far less attention: designing AI to help people by [...] Many health communicators assume that those who learn the facts will pursue healthier choices. AI is now being built on the same assumption, which ignores how messages actually influence behavior. Messages, like medicines, can help, harm, or do nothing at all, and the only way to know which is to test them.

items.title: Banks push online banking, then blame us when we get hacked | Opinion
items.summary:
People – some of us, at least – are worried about AI eventually overthrowing human civilization. Even more immediately, there's widespread concern about the proliferation of data centers needed to support AI operations.

Yet at the same time we're collectively wringing our hands about those issues, we are meekly surrendering more and more control to machines over our everyday lives. [...] One theory about an AI Armageddon doesn't involve robots who look like Arnold Schwarzenegger hunting us down with laser guns. AI could just take over our natural habitat, as we've done with other animals and plants, which would leave us without food and shelter.

Here's a thought exercise: If AI were evaluating whether humans were worth saving for conservation purposes, would we grade out more as an invasive species or one that made important contributions to the ecosystem? [...] For that matter, we're starting to trust AI to give us authoritative answers to all of life's questions, including those where human moral judgments and lived experiences might guide us better.

After all, why bother doing any research on our own when we can just type a question into a search field and have some chatbot spit out a near-instantaneous response?

items.title: Accurate medical advice from AI can still be dangerous | STAT
items.summary: Artificial intelligence is delivering health guidance at an unprecedented scale. Every week, more than 300 million people ask ChatGPT health questions. Now, the federal government is moving AI deeper into medical care to communicate directly and autonomously with patients. Chris Klomp, the nominee for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, has called AI in patient care the agency’s “holy grail” for improving the nation’s health. [...] Medical ethics pairs the duty to do no harm with beneficence, which is an affirmative obligation to do good. Safety evaluations of AI have focused mainly on the first duty by screening for responses that encourage imminent self-harm, discourage necessary care, or spread false information. Behavioral benchmarking would extend the first duty beyond imminent danger to long-term harms. It could also advance the second duty, which has received far less attention: designing AI to help people by [...] Many health communicators assume that those who learn the facts will pursue healthier choices. AI is now being built on the same assumption, which ignores how messages actually influence behavior. Messages, like medicines, can help, harm, or do nothing at all, and the only way to know which is to test them.

items.title: Banks push online banking, then blame us when we get hacked | Opinion

People – some of us, at least – are worried about AI eventually overthrowing human civilization. Even more immediately, there's widespread concern about the proliferation of data centers needed to support AI operations.

Yet at the same time we're collectively wringing our hands about those issues, we are meekly surrendering more and more control to machines over our everyday lives. [...] One theory about an AI Armageddon doesn't involve robots who look like Arnold Schwarzenegger hunting us down with laser guns. AI could just take over our natural habitat, as we've done with other animals and plants, which would leave us without food and shelter.

Here's a thought exercise: If AI were evaluating whether humans were worth saving for conservation purposes, would we grade out more as an invasive species or one that made important contributions to the ecosystem? [...] For that matter, we're starting to trust AI to give us authoritative answers to all of life's questions, including those where human moral judgments and lived experiences might guide us better.

After all, why bother doing any research on our own when we can just type a question into a search field and have some chatbot spit out a near-instantaneous response?

Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which specializes in logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the new methods earlier this year to analyze parcel sorting data and test updates to robot behavior. Tests showed an increased capacity of over 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot; the change is now deployed across 30% of the company’s U.S. fleet. [...] Ken Goldberg

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are controlled,” Goldberg said. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are coming for the development workflow | InfoWorld
items.summary: This is clearly where the frontier labs are moving, even though they’ve all benefited from an industry that provided neutral spaces to build. For example, OpenAI developed Pando, a Git back end for its own monorepo, to handle more engineers and agents reading and writing code concurrently. Its engineers kept using Git. OpenAI retained compatibility with the protocol and client and contributed improvements upstream. That compatibility let it rebuild the back end around the way its engineers [...] This pressure to maximize profitability helps explain why frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are aggressively adding functionality to own more of the developer’s workflow. On November 4, OpenAI announced an agreement to buy Pierre, the company behind Code Storage and the open source libraries Codex already uses to browse files and review changes. OpenAI wants Codex to be where developers work, from the first branch an agent creates through deployment of the application. There’s money in [...] OpenAI or Anthropic could build the place developers prefer to work. The question is what happens when a team likes that place and wants a rival’s agent for a particular job. Maybe a startup has built a tool that can track down the intermittent test failure that’s had the team stumped for a week. Give it access to the code and test history the team has authorized, and it gets a chance to prove itself. Ask the team to move its work to a new platform first, and it probably never gets to try.

# Australia to launch AI safety regulator after OpenAI’s breach of a government portal

By 

ROD McGUIRK

The Associated Press

MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by a rogue OpenAI agent in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday. [...] OpenAI apologized in September for the breach and its slow response.

“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a statement. “We also should have handled our response better.”

## Inquiry recommends possible criminal law changes

A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations including that the government consider changing the law. [...] Albanese told OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman that the U.S. company took too long to inform the government in September that a rogue agent had infiltrated government websites three months earlier, which was the first occurrence of such a breach with the technology.

Advertising

Information taken without authorization from the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18 has since been made public. It is not clear whether the portal breach broke any Australian laws.
